title: Phased T2T horse and donkey assemblies from a mule reveal peculiar equid centromere evolution.
data_url: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_041296265.1/ (horse TB-T2T) and GCF_041296235.1 (donkey EquAss-T2T_v2); supplementary tables via Europe PMC PMC13477059

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC search on the DOI returned exactly 1 hit (PMID 42561953, PMC13477059, open access, licence CC BY-NC-ND); I downloaded the full text XML (255,911 bytes) and read the Results, 'Data and code availability', 'Web access of source and derived datasets' and all STAR Methods subsections. I downloaded the Europe PMC supplementary bundle (22,951,233 bytes, 9 files) and wrote my own pure-Python xlsx reader to parse every spreadsheet, because this laptop has no pandas. (1) mmc3.xlsx = Table S2, satellite families: 19 rows, columns Species / Satellite family / Monomer length / Reference / Consensus sequence, with the full consensus DNA sequence of each family present as text. (2) mmc4.xlsx = Table S3, horse satellite loci: columns chr / start / end / length / satellite family, 1,752 data rows, zero empty cells in any column, zero duplicate (chr,start,end) triples, and end minus start equals the stated length in all 1,752 rows. Family counts I computed: 2PI 937, CENPB-sat 643, 37cen 69, EC137 43, SatB 33, SatA 27. Total 246,712,982 base pairs, which is 9.19% of the 2,683,570,634 base pairs of assembled horse chromosomes (the paper says 'about 9%'). 646 loci are at least 10 kilobases long, 196 at least 100 kilobases. (3) mmc5.xlsx = Table S4, donkey satellite loci: same five columns, 3,456 data rows, again no missing values, no duplicate coordinates, length column internally consistent. Family counts: SatA 2,410, 2PI 316, SatC 292, CENPB-sat 168, SatB 95, 2PI-telo 90, 37cen 72, EC137 7, SatD 6. Total 224,293,737 base pairs = 8.32% of the 2,695,841,206 base pairs of assembled donkey chromosomes (the paper says 8.3%, an exact match). (4) mmc7.xlsx = Table S6: 374 horse ribosomal RNA gene rows (28S 128, 5.8S 124, 18S 122). (5) mmc8.xlsx = Table S7: 1,140 donkey ribosomal RNA gene rows. (6) mmc6.xlsx = Table S5, transposable element annotation: 196 real data rows (49 element subclasses x 4 assemblies) x 56 columns, plus one repeated header row sitting inside the data block. Combined labelled satellite loci across both species: 5,208. I then cross-checked the coordinates against the real assemblies using the NCBI Datasets application programming interface: horse GCF_041296265.1 'TB-T2T' is 2,769,438,211 base pairs, 32 chromosomes, 624 scaffolds, contig N50 99,223,387, BUSCO (a gene-completeness score) 99.08% complete, RefSeq-annotated with 39,335 genes; donkey GCF_041296235.1 'EquAss-T2T_v2' is 2,797,756,172 base pairs, 31 chromosomes. No satellite locus in either table runs past the end of its chromosome. I also found a real identifier trap: 363 of the 1,752 horse rows (20.7%, 36,687,968 base pairs) put a chromosome accession in the chr column (NC_091701.1, NC_091702.1, NC_091703.1, NC_091705.1, NC_091714.1) while the coordinates actually belong to five separate unplaced scaffolds; I confirmed this by paging all 625 sequence records of the horse assembly and checking that each group's largest coordinate fits inside the matching scaffold but not the chromosome (for example 12,861,650 fits inside NW_027222394.1 at 12,873,522; 5,527,243 fits inside NW_027222343.1 at 5,541,805), and by finding 45 coordinate pairs that overlap between the 'chr18/19/20/22/31' rows and the 'NC_...' rows for the same chromosome number. Within chromosomes I also counted 150 overlapping locus pairs of which 126 are completely nested inside a larger locus. Finally I confirmed by HTTP HEAD request only (not download, both far over my 50 MB limit) that the two genome sequence files are 822,142,827 and 826,898,623 bytes compressed, freely served from the NCBI file server with no login.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the centromeres themselves. I could not read either supplementary PDF (this machine has no PDF renderer and the embedded fonts use custom subset encodings, so raw text extraction returned only glyph codes), so Table S1 (per-chromosome assembly statistics, telomere and gap descriptions), Tables S8-S10 (software list, mule tissue list, sequencing statistics) and all of Methods S1 (mmc2.pdf, 9,946,474 bytes, the per-chromosome CENP-A chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing profile panels) are paper-text-only for me. Taken from text: that CENP-A (centromere protein A, the protein that marks where a centromere is) was measured by chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing in ten horses and four donkeys; that the horse has exactly one satellite-free centromere (chromosome 11) and 31 satellite-based ones, and the donkey 16 satellite-free and 15 satellite-based; that CENP-A peak positions move between individuals within a 500 kilobase window in the horse and up to a 2.8 megabase window on donkey chromosome 12; that CENP-B binding is dissociated from CENP-A at equid centromeres; and the chromosome-alignment and rearrangement findings. I verified independently that none of these centromere positions appears as a coordinate in any deposited machine-readable file.

a1_downloadable.note: Fully open, no login and no access application. I pulled all nine supplementary files from Europe PMC myself, and both genome assemblies are public RefSeq reference genomes. Two practical frictions I hit: PMC's own per-file supplementary links sit behind an automated proof-of-work bot check (I did not work around it), and the Europe PMC bundle took about six minutes to transfer. The genome sequence files are 822 MB and 827 MB compressed, over my 50 MB download rule, so I recorded their size by HTTP header rather than downloading.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS, and this is the killer. The thing this paper is about, and the only target worth modelling here, is where the centromere actually sits on each chromosome. That is nowhere a column: the CENP-A (centromere protein A) enrichment profiles exist only as plotted panels inside a 9.9 MB PDF and as raw sequencing reads in the Sequence Read Archive (PRJNA1354467 plus previously published run accessions). To get a label you would have to align roughly 24 chromatin immunoprecipitation libraries against two 2.8-gigabase genomes and call enrichment domains yourself, which is exactly the 'construct the thing you are predicting' failure, and the paper states plainly that no code was deposited. The one label column that does exist, 'satellite family', is a different and much weaker target - see A8.

a3_inputs_present.note: Passes, narrowly, with a trap. The feature would be DNA sequence, and the tables carry only coordinates, not sequence. But it is 63 chromosome sequences to fetch, not thousands of lookups, and they come in two bulk files. The trap I verified: 363 of 1,752 horse rows name a chromosome accession (NC_091701.1 and four others) whose coordinates really belong to five separate unplaced scaffolds (NW_027222394.1 and four others, resolvable only via Table 1 of the paper). Anyone slicing sequence by the accession printed in the file would silently get the wrong DNA for 21% of horse rows.

a4_units_stated.note: Effectively fine. Coordinates and lengths are base pairs; the unit is implied by the header rather than stated, but I confirmed end minus start equals the length column in all 5,208 rows and that no coordinate exceeds its chromosome, so there is no ambiguity. One unstated convention: adjacent merged loci share a boundary value (one locus ends at 1,835,650 and the next begins at 1,835,650), which means the coordinates are the 0-based half-open style used by the BED file format - an off-by-one risk for anyone who assumes otherwise.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS for the real target. The paper describes 32 horse centromeres and 31 donkey centromeres, so 63 labelled examples - far under the ~400 the checklist requires even for pure classification, and the useful contrast (satellite-free versus satellite-based) is 17 versus 46. The satellite-locus tables do have enough rows (1,752 horse + 3,456 donkey = 5,208, a count I made myself), but those rows carry the wrong label (A8). Note also that the whole resource is two individuals, one horse and one donkey, so the effective sample size for anything genomic is 2.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 1.65 GB of compressed genome sequence (about 5.6 GB uncompressed), reducible to roughly 0.5 GB if you keep only windows around the 5,208 annotated satellite loci; the supplementary tables themselves are 0.4 MB
a6_fits_laptop.note: Would fit with ordinary streaming: read one chromosome at a time (the largest is 209 megabases, so under 1 GB of memory), cut out the annotated windows, discard the rest. No graphics card needed for a small DNA language model on a few thousand short windows. This is the one size-filter item the resource survives, but only because you throw away 99% of it; by CLAUDE.md's size rule this is still a genomics-scale assembly resource and is scored down accordingly.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The headline numbers reconcile, which is to the authors' credit. My own sum of the donkey table gives 8.32% of assembled chromosome length as satellite, against the paper's stated 8.3%; the horse gives 9.19% against 'about 9%'. What does not reconcile is naming, not counting: the Table S3 caption says the extra rows come from five contigs and labels them with chromosome accessions, while the Methods name five scaffold accessions instead, and Table 1 adds a footnote saying 'All accession numbers reference GenBank accessions' when every accession printed is in fact a RefSeq accession.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAILS for the fallback target, in the most literal way the checklist describes. The 'satellite family' label was produced by running RepeatMasker, an alignment program, against a library of the family consensus sequences that are themselves printed in Table S2 - so the label is a deterministic function of the very DNA sequence that would be the model's input. Predicting it is distilling RepeatMasker, not learning biology, and a plain alignment to the nine consensus sequences reproduces it essentially perfectly. The CENP-A centromere labels, by contrast, have excellent provenance (a real antibody pull-down measurement in 14 animals) - they are just not in any file.

existing_models.name: dna-brnn (an open neural network that labels centromeric satellite repeats base by base, from Heng Li, 2019)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported to match RepeatMasker closely while running much faster, with a false-negative rate of roughly 0.3% for the HSat2,3 human satellite class on the independently assembled CHM1 human genome (trained on human decoy sequence, tested on a different assembly). Fewer than 5,000 free parameters. Read from the paper and its abstract, not re-run by me.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The method only distinguishes two broad satellite classes (alpha satellite and HSat2,3); extending it to many families, and to species other than human, is left open.

existing_models.name: DeepGRP (an open tool that annotates repetitive genomic elements with a recurrent neural network plus an attention mechanism, 2021)
existing_models.score_and_split: Presented as an engineering improvement over dna-brnn for nucleotide-level annotation of repeat elements; I read only the abstract and summaries and so quote no accuracy number.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - I did not open the primary paper.

existing_models.name: centroAnno (an open 2025 algorithm that annotates centromeres and tandem repeats from assembly sequence with no template required)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported repeat annotation rates above 0.9 across all tested centromeric regions, versus below 0.8 for the TRASH tool on human centromere 15, and it recovered repeat unit lengths matching the known 171 base pair alpha-satellite ground truth. Code at github.com/junhaiqi/centroAnno. Read from the bioRxiv preprint summary.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: They frame competitor tools (HORmon, HiCAT) as needing known centromere sequences and monomer templates, and note cases where those tools miss repeat types; fine-scale limits are not something I retrieved verbatim.

existing_models.name: HiCAT (an open tool for automatic annotation of centromere higher-order repeat structure, Genome Biology 2023) and SatXplor (an open satellite-DNA analysis pipeline, Briefings in Bioinformatics 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Both are published, open pipelines for exactly the task of describing satellite arrays in a finished assembly. I read titles and abstracts only and quote no number.

existing_models.name: A sequence-based predictor of where CENP-A actually binds (that is, a model for the paper's real question)
existing_models.score_and_split: I found none in four searches. Searching is weak evidence, so call this likely absent rather than absent - but there is a strong biological reason for the gap, which several of the papers I found state outright: CENP-A binding position is epigenetic, not sequence-determined, and in this very dataset the binding position moves between individuals of the same species by up to 2.8 megabases on identical DNA. A sequence-only model is close to logically impossible here.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The equid literature names the mechanism of centromere sliding and epiallele inheritance as unsolved, but explicitly as a chromatin problem, not a sequence problem.

backbone.name: Nucleotide Transformer or DNABERT-2 (DNA language models with open weights on Hugging Face) would be the right shape for classifying short genomic windows, and HyenaDNA could take megabase-long windows. All three are genuinely available and would run on this laptop for a few thousand windows.
backbone.hardware: Central processing unit only: about 5,208 windows of a few kilobases through a small DNA language model is a couple of hours of one-time embedding, then seconds per cross-validation fold. The backbone is not the problem here; the label is.
backbone.licence: Nucleotide Transformer and HyenaDNA weights are permissively licensed. The assemblies are public-domain NCBI data. The paper itself is CC BY-NC-ND, which restricts redistributing the article but not reusing the deposited data.

integration.partner_dataset: The RefSeq gene annotation that NCBI already built on these same two assemblies (39,335 horse genes, released December 2024), and the cohort of 185 North American Thoroughbred horses from Bailey et al. 2024 whose sequences the authors say they have mapped to this new reference and posted as alignment and variant files.
integration.join_key: Genomic coordinates on a named genome build (TB-T2T / GCF_041296265.1 or EquAss-T2T_v2 / GCF_041296235.1). The key is clean and standard, with one caveat I verified: 363 horse rows print a chromosome accession but hold scaffold coordinates, so 21% of that join would silently land on the wrong sequence unless you repair it from Table 1 of the paper.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does satellite-array composition predict which chromosome regions are gene-poor and rearrangement-prone across 185 sequenced Thoroughbreds? It is a real question, but the horse variant files are distributed as alignment and variant files on a university web page rather than a repository, and with 32 chromosomes as the unit of analysis there is not enough to fit anything - so the join is interesting to a geneticist and useless to a model.

controls.positive_control: Would have been strong if the labels existed: predict the length of each satellite locus from its sequence (trivially learnable, must come out near-perfect), and check that a model recovers the textbook fact that 37cen arrays sit at horse centromeres while CENPB-sat sits beside them. Both are stated in advance in the paper.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the satellite-family label and confirm collapse to the majority class (2PI is 53% of horse rows, SatA is 70% of donkey rows, so the dummy baseline is already high); and hold out whole chromosomes rather than individual loci, since loci inside one array are near-identical copies and a random split would leak outright.
controls.external_validation: Genuinely good and cheap, which is the frustrating part: the two species are independent, so you can train on horse and test on donkey, and two older assemblies of the same species (EquCab3.0 and ASM1607732v2) are already tabulated in Table S5 for a platform-change check. There is no year or source column, so no temporal split.

honest_claim_h3: The most a model built on what is actually deposited could honestly claim is: 'given a stretch of horse or donkey chromosome, this reproduces the satellite family that RepeatMasker assigned to it when aligned against nine published consensus sequences, in one horse and one donkey' - which is a statement about an alignment program's output on two animals, not about centromere biology.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a stretch of horse or donkey chromosome sequence to predict whether the cell builds its centromere there.
plain_idea.train_on: Intended: windows of DNA sequence from two gapless genomes, labelled by whether the centromere protein actually binds there. Actually available: 5,208 satellite-repeat locations (1,752 horse, 3,456 donkey - counts I made myself), each with chromosome, start, end, length and a repeat-family name, plus two freely downloadable 2.8-billion-base genome sequences.
plain_idea.predict: Whether a given piece of chromosome is the functional centromere. The true answer would come from pulling down CENP-A, the protein that marks centromeres, with an antibody and sequencing what came with it - done here in ten horses and four donkeys, but published only as pictures, so there is no answer key to train against.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Equid chromosomes are the textbook case where centromere position and repetitive DNA have come apart, so anyone studying how centromeres are chosen, and horse breeders' genome projects, would want a sequence-based predictor. Even a failure would be informative, because it would quantify how little of centromere position is written in the DNA.

ml_idea: Two framings, and both die. (1) The project the paper invites: predict centromere position, or CENP-A (centromere protein A) binding, from DNA sequence, and ask whether a model trained on horse transfers to donkey. This is a genuinely good question and the data behind it is a real physical measurement in 14 animals - but the measurement is deposited only as raw sequencing reads in the Sequence Read Archive and as plotted panels in a 9.9 MB PDF, so the label would have to be built from scratch by aligning roughly 24 libraries to two 2.8-gigabase genomes, with no code released. And the unit is the centromere: 32 in the horse, 31 in the donkey, 63 in total, against the checklist's ~400 floor. Worse, the paper's own result argues the task is close to impossible, because CENP-A position shifts by up to 2.8 megabases between individuals carrying the same DNA. (2) The fallback the files do support: predict satellite family from sequence over 5,208 clean, fully populated rows. The table is genuinely model-ready - no missing values, no duplicate coordinates, lengths internally consistent, totals matching the paper to within 0.01 percentage points on the donkey - but the label was computed by running RepeatMasker against the nine consensus sequences printed in Table S2, so it is a deterministic function of the input, and the field already has dna-brnn, DeepGRP, centroAnno, HiCAT and SatXplor, all open. There is a real, small finding to salvage and report: 363 of the 1,752 horse rows (20.7%, 36.7 megabases) carry a chromosome accession in the chr column while their coordinates belong to five different unplaced scaffolds, so anyone extracting sequence from Table S3 as printed gets the wrong DNA for a fifth of the horse rows, and the per-family base-pair totals quietly include 45 overlapping and 126 fully nested intervals. That is a half-page note to the authors, not a project.

effort.compute_note: working_set_gb is the measured compressed size of the two genome files (822,142,827 + 826,898,623 bytes, from HTTP headers, not downloaded). peak_ram_gb assumes you stream one chromosome at a time; the largest is 209 megabases, so well under a gigabyte of string. embedding_hours assumes 5,208 windows at roughly one to two seconds each through a small DNA language model on this laptop's processor - an estimate, nothing timed. hours_to_feature_table covers repairing the 363 mislabelled accessions, deciding what to do with 126 nested intervals, and extracting sequence; I spent about an hour parsing the tables and verifying coordinates, so the rest is extrapolation.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Grep every deposited file for a column holding centromere or CENP-A coordinates. There is none - the only label column in 0.4 MB of spreadsheets is 'satellite family', which RepeatMasker computed from the sequence itself. Five minutes. The second-cheapest check is to count centromeres: 32 plus 31 is 63, which ends the discussion.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A at A2, A5 and A8, in three independent ways I checked in the files rather than inferring from the abstract. A2: the paper's real target, where the centromere sits, is not a column anywhere - the CENP-A (centromere protein A) measurements from ten horses and four donkeys are deposited only as raw reads in the Sequence Read Archive and as plotted panels in a 9.9 MB PDF, with no code released, so the label would have to be constructed by aligning roughly 24 libraries to two 2.8-gigabase genomes. A5: the unit of analysis is the centromere, and there are 63 of them (32 horse, 31 donkey), from exactly two animals. A8: the only ready-made label column, 'satellite family' across 5,208 loci, was produced by running RepeatMasker against the nine consensus sequences printed in Table S2, so it is a deterministic function of the input sequence - leakage by construction, and the task is already served by at least five open tools (dna-brnn, DeepGRP, centroAnno, HiCAT, SatXplor). The resource itself is excellent and the deposit is honest: both assemblies are public RefSeq reference genomes with BUSCO 99.08% completeness, the supplementary tables parsed on the first try with zero missing values and zero duplicate coordinates, and my own sums reproduce the paper's satellite fractions (8.32% donkey against their 8.3%, 9.19% horse against their 'about 9%'). By CLAUDE.md's size filter it is also a genomics-scale assembly resource: 1.65 GB of compressed sequence before any subsetting. Two file-level defects worth reporting back to the authors, both verified by me: 363 of 1,752 horse rows (20.7%, 36.7 megabases) print a chromosome accession in the chr column while their coordinates belong to five separate unplaced scaffolds, and the per-family totals include 45 overlapping and 126 fully nested intervals. Finally, the paper's own central finding - that CENP-A position slides up to 2.8 megabases between individuals with the same DNA - is itself an argument that the interesting prediction task cannot be done from sequence.
